question:
The six children listed below are from two families of three siblings each. Each child has blue or brown eyes and black or blond hair. Children from the same family have at least one of these characteristics in common. Which two children are Jim’s siblings?

\[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Child} & \text{Eye Color} & \text{Hair Color}\\ \hline \text{Benjamin} & \text{Blue} & \text{Black}\\ \hline \text{Jim} & \text{Brown} & \text{Blond}\\ \hline \text{Nadeen} & \text{Brown} & \text{Black}\\ \hline \text{Austin} & \text{Blue} & \text{Blond}\\ \hline \text{Tevyn} & \text{Blue} & \text{Black}\\ \hline \text{Sue} & \text{Blue} & \text{Blond}\\ \hline\end{array}\]
solution:
Jim has brown eyes and blond hair. Benjamin and Tevyn both have blue eyes and black hair, so neither shares a characteristic with Jim. Therefore Jim’s two siblings must come from Nadeen, Austin, and Sue.

Nadeen cannot be in the same family as either Austin or Sue: her brown eyes and black hair match neither their blue eyes nor their blond hair. If Nadeen were Jim’s sibling, there would be no possible third child for their family. Thus Jim’s siblings must be Austin and Sue.

This grouping satisfies the conditions: Jim, Austin, and Sue share blond hair, while Benjamin, Nadeen, and Tevyn share black hair. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{Austin and Sue}}\), choice \(\text{E}\).

edges.reason: Knowing 6 to 10 broadens which everyday collections can be described. The actual project gives no required range, so Gemini adds an unlisted up-to-ten obligation; small counts and the sorting criterion can be addressed independently.

Both external rejections assume every category is small, but the source states no count bound.
